paragraphs.title: Opening of the Prayer and Divine Revelation

answers: A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet upon Shigionoth
A song of David about war
easy.explanation: Verse 1 calls it “A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet upon Shigionoth.”

answers: Revive it and make it known
easy.explanation: He asks, “revive thy work” and “make known” it in the midst of the years.
easy.q: What does Habakkuk ask God to do with His work?

easy.explanation: The verse concludes, “in wrath remember mercy.”
easy.q: What does Habakkuk ask God to remember in wrath?

medium.explanation: Verse 3 says, “His glory covered the heavens.”
medium.q: What covered the heavens when God appeared?

medium.explanation: Verse 4 says, “his brightness was as the light.”
medium.q: What was God’s brightness compared to?

medium.explanation: The verse says, “there was the hiding of his power.”
medium.q: What was hidden in the radiance?

answers: God is revealed in brightness, yet His power is hidden
God does not appear at all
God appears only through human rulers
challenge.explanation: God’s glory and brightness are visible, while “the hiding of his power” is also mentioned.
challenge.q: What central tension appears in the description of God’s revelation?

answers: Prayer, request for revival, and description of revelation
challenge.explanation: The passage begins with a prayer, presents Habakkuk’s request, and then describes God’s appearance.
challenge.q: What is the main progression in verses 1–4?

answers: Mercy is requested even during judgment
Wrath should be directed only at the prophet
challenge.explanation: Habakkuk asks God to remember mercy while exercising wrath.
challenge.q: What does “in wrath remember mercy” imply?

paragraphs.title: The World Shaken by God's Warlike Appearance

easy.explanation: Verse 5 says, “Before him went the pestilence.”

answers: The mountains were scattered and the nations were driven apart
easy.explanation: God drove the nations apart, and the everlasting mountains were scattered.
easy.q: What happened to the everlasting mountains and nations?

answers: His horses and chariots of salvation
easy.explanation: Verse 8 asks about riding “upon thine horses and thy chariots of salvation.”

medium.explanation: They are called “thy chariots of salvation.”
medium.q: What do the chariots represent in the passage?

medium.explanation: Verse 9 says, “Thy bow was made quite naked.”
The verse says, “Thou didst cleave the earth with rivers.”
medium.q: What did God cleave the earth with?

answers: As a force of war that shakes the natural and political order
As a private meeting without earthly effects
challenge.explanation: Pestilence, burning coals, scattered mountains, divided nations, horses, chariots, and a bow create a warlike picture.
challenge.q: How is God’s appearance portrayed in verses 5–9?

answers: Both are shaken by God’s appearing
They are unrelated in the passage
challenge.explanation: The earth, mountains, and nations all respond to God’s overwhelming power.
challenge.q: What connection exists between nature and the nations in this passage?

answers: God’s action is connected with fulfilling His covenant purposes
The passage has no reference to tribes
challenge.explanation: God’s exposed bow is described in connection with “the oaths of the tribes.”
challenge.q: What do the “oaths of the tribes” suggest in context?

paragraphs.title: Nature Trembles and the Enemies Are Defeated

easy.explanation: Verse 11 says, “The sun and moon stood still in their habitation.”
Verse 12 says, “thou didst thresh the heathen in anger.”
easy.q: What did God do to the heathen?

answers: For the salvation of His people and His anointed
easy.explanation: Verse 13 says He went forth “for the salvation of thy people.”

answers: The mountains trembled and the deep uttered its voice
medium.explanation: The mountains trembled, and “the deep uttered his voice.”
medium.q: How did the mountains and deep respond?

answers: Mountains and waters, then sun and moon, then land and sea
medium.explanation: The passage moves through mountains, waters, heavenly bodies, land, and sea.
medium.q: Which sequence best describes the passage?

medium.explanation: The KJV says, “The sun and moon stood still in their habitation.”
medium.q: Where did the sun and moon stand?

challenge.explanation: These active verbs describe nature reacting to God’s appearing.
challenge.q: What shows that nature is portrayed as responding to God?

answers: God saves His people while defeating the house of the wicked
Salvation is entirely separate from conflict
challenge.explanation: The same divine action brings salvation to God’s people and judgment on the wicked.
challenge.q: How are salvation and defeat connected?

answers: He marches through it and threshes the heathen
The deep is mentioned without any action
challenge.explanation: The verbs “march” and “thresh” present direct and powerful action.
challenge.q: What emphasizes the force of God’s action upon the land?

paragraphs.title: The Prophet's Fear and the Land's Devastation

answers: His belly trembled and he quivered
easy.explanation: He says, “My belly trembled” and “my lips quivered.”
easy.q: What happened to Habakkuk’s body when he heard the vision?

easy.explanation: He says he trembled “that I might rest in the day of trouble.”
easy.q: For what day did Habakkuk wait?

easy.explanation: Verse 17 begins, “Although the fig tree shall not blossom.”

answers: It includes crops, fruit, flocks, and herds
medium.explanation: The verse names figs, vines, olives, fields, sheep, and cattle.
medium.q: How extensive is the deprivation in verse 17?

answers: The land’s condition makes him rejoice
medium.explanation: The passage moves from Habakkuk’s bodily terror to a description of widespread devastation.
medium.q: How does the prophet’s fear relate to the land’s condition?

medium.explanation: The KJV says, “the fields shall yield no meat.”

answers: The deprivation is comprehensive, not limited to one crop
Only one branch of agriculture failed
challenge.explanation: The verse lists failures of fruit, vines, olives, fields, sheep, and cattle.
challenge.q: What does the list of losses in verse 17 show?

answers: Hearing the message produces trembling and terror
challenge.explanation: After saying “When I heard,” Habakkuk describes trembling, quivering, and rottenness in his bones.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between “When I heard” and Habakkuk’s physical response?

answers: The vision displays divine power, while the prophet responds with human fear
The vision is peaceful, while the prophet celebrates
The vision concerns harvest, while the prophet ignores it
challenge.explanation: The overwhelming revelation causes Habakkuk deep physical fear.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between the vision and Habakkuk’s response?

paragraphs.title: Rejoicing in God and the Believer's Strength

answers: The LORD and the God of his salvation
easy.explanation: He says, “I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.”
easy.q: In whom does Habakkuk choose to rejoice?

easy.explanation: Verse 19 says, “The LORD God is my strength.”
easy.q: What does Habakkuk call the Lord God?

answers: The chief singer and stringed instruments
easy.explanation: The verse ends, “To the chief singer on my stringed instruments.”
easy.q: What was the song intended for?

answers: Trust in the LORD and His salvation
medium.explanation: He chooses joy in God even after describing famine and loss.
medium.q: What enables Habakkuk to rejoice despite the deprivation?

medium.explanation: The LORD will make his feet “like hinds’ feet.”
medium.q: What will God make Habakkuk’s feet like?

answers: God is Habakkuk’s source of power
medium.explanation: Calling the LORD his strength means Habakkuk relies on Him for power and endurance.
medium.q: What does “my strength” mean in this context?

answers: Habakkuk moves from fear and deprivation to trust, joy, and strength
He moves from joy to fear only
He moves from harvest to military planning
challenge.explanation: After trembling and describing loss, he chooses to rejoice and declares God to be his strength.
challenge.q: What is the main change between verses 16–17 and verses 18–19?

answers: It suggests agility and confident movement over difficult heights
It describes a shortage of animals
It removes the need for God’s guidance
challenge.explanation: God enables Habakkuk to walk securely upon high places.
challenge.q: How does the image of hinds’ feet support the idea of faith?

answers: It presents the passage as a prayer or song for performance
It changes the passage into a legal code
challenge.explanation: The closing direction assigns the song to the chief singer and stringed instruments.
challenge.q: What is the function of the musical ending?
